# Overview

{strainselect} helps choosing which bacterial strains to sequence from a
collection described by metadata (sampling context, matrix, region, sector,
year...). It offers two complementary methods:

- the **clustering method** (`assess_gower()`, `cstats_table()`,
  `select_silhouette()`) is suited when the number of strains that can be
  sequenced is limited. Strains are grouped into *k* clusters of similar
  strains and the best clustered strain of each cluster is selected, so that
  the selected strains are as different as possible from each other;
- the **profile method** (`prepare_upset()`, `define_profiles()`,
  `select_profiles()`) is suited when the number of strains to sequence is
  not limited. Strains sharing exactly the same metadata are grouped and one
  strain per group is selected, so that every distinct profile — including
  unique strains — is represented.

Both methods start with `prepare_input()`, which cleans the raw table.

The examples below use `salmonella_strains`, a table of 100 *Salmonella*
strains described by 22 variables, shipped with the package. The selection is
based on 6 variables: `CONTEXTE`, `MATRICE1`, `REGION`, `SECTEUR`, `LIEUPVT`
and the year extracted from `DATE_PRELEVEMENT`.

# Example data: salmonella_strains

`salmonella_strains` is available as soon as the package is loaded. The same
table is also shipped as a CSV file (`;` separator), which shows the expected
format of an input file:
`system.file("data_test.csv", package = "strainselect")`.

```{r examples-salmonella_strains}
str(salmonella_strains[, c("IDENTIFIANT", "CONTEXTE", "REGION", "DATE_PRELEVEMENT")])
```

# Preparing the data: prepare_input

Before using any of the methods, the dataset must be cleaned and contain only
the metadata on which the selection is based. `prepare_input()`:

- checks that strain identifiers are unique (and stops with the list of
  duplicated identifiers otherwise);
- uses the identifiers as row names;
- keeps only the selected metadata columns;
- optionally extracts the year (`ANNEE`) and/or the month (`MOIS`) from a date
  column;
- replaces missing values by `"unknown"` and converts every column to a factor.

Columns can be given by their names (recommended, as it is easier to read and
does not depend on the order of the columns) or by their positions. Dates are
read with `date_format`, `"%d/%m/%Y"` (e.g. `09/01/2020`) by default; use for
instance `date_format = "%Y-%m-%d"` for dates such as `2020-01-09`. A date
column already of class `Date` is used as is.

```{r examples-prepare_input}
raw_data <- salmonella_strains
prepared_data <- prepare_input(
  raw_data,
  col_select = c("CONTEXTE", "MATRICE1", "REGION", "SECTEUR", "LIEUPVT"),
  id = "IDENTIFIANT", date = "DATE_PRELEVEMENT", month = FALSE, year = TRUE
)
head(prepared_data)
# the same with column positions
prepared_data <- prepare_input(raw_data, col_select = c(5, 8, 11, 12, 15, 22),
                               id = 1, date = 15)
```

# Clustering method

The clustering method uses three functions: `assess_gower()`,
`cstats_table()` and `select_silhouette()`. `cstats_table()` is optional when
the number of strains to sequence is fixed in advance.

## Distances and tree: assess_gower

`assess_gower()` computes a dissimilarity matrix between strains using the
Gower distance, which is suited to categorical metadata. Weights can be given
to the metadata to adjust their importance in the clustering. A hierarchical
clustering with complete linkage is then performed on this matrix, and the
dendrogram is drawn when `graph = TRUE`.

```{r examples-assess_gower}
raw_data <- salmonella_strains
prepared_data <- prepare_input(raw_data, col_select = c("CONTEXTE", "MATRICE1", "REGION", "SECTEUR", "LIEUPVT"),
                               id = "IDENTIFIANT", date = "DATE_PRELEVEMENT")
gower <- assess_gower(prepared_data, graph = TRUE)
```

## Choosing the number of clusters: cstats_table

`cstats_table()` computes clustering statistics (see `fpc::cluster.stats()`)
for an increasing number of clusters: `step`, `2 * step`, ..., up to `k`. The
average silhouette width (`avg.silwidth`) is the most useful one: it is
plotted against the number of clusters, and the optimal number of clusters is
marked by a maximum or a plateau of the curve. The idea is to test a large
number of clusters without exceeding the number of strains that can be
sequenced; a larger `step` reduces the computing time.

```{r examples-cstats_table}
raw_data <- salmonella_strains
prepared_data <- prepare_input(raw_data, col_select = c("CONTEXTE", "MATRICE1", "REGION", "SECTEUR", "LIEUPVT"),
                               id = "IDENTIFIANT", date = "DATE_PRELEVEMENT")
gower <- assess_gower(prepared_data, graph = FALSE)
stats <- cstats_table(dist = gower$gower_dist, tree = gower$aggl.clust.c,
                      k = 50, step = 10)
stats[, c("cluster.number", "avg.silwidth")]
```

## Selecting the strains: select_silhouette

The last step selects one strain to sequence in each cluster. The number of
clusters `k` is either chosen from the silhouette plot or set to the number of
strains that can be sequenced. For each cluster, the strain with the largest
silhouette width — i.e. the best clustered strain — is selected. When several
strains share the largest silhouette width in a cluster, one of them is chosen
at random; use `seed` to make this choice reproducible.

```{r examples-select_silhouette}
raw_data <- salmonella_strains
prepared_data <- prepare_input(raw_data, col_select = c("CONTEXTE", "MATRICE1", "REGION", "SECTEUR", "LIEUPVT"),
                               id = "IDENTIFIANT", date = "DATE_PRELEVEMENT")
gower <- assess_gower(prepared_data, graph = FALSE)
selection <- select_silhouette(prepared_data, dist = gower$gower_dist, k = 20,
                               seed = 1)
# the 20 strains to sequence
unique(selection$selected)
```

# Selecting strains for a sequencing budget: select_strains

`select_strains()` runs the whole clustering method in one step and answers
the practical question "*I can sequence at most `n_max` strains: which ones?*".

1. It computes the Gower distances and the clustering tree (as
   `assess_gower()`), then the average silhouette width for every number of
   clusters from 2 to the number of distinct profiles. The number of clusters
   with the largest average silhouette width is the **optimal number of
   clusters** `k_opt`.
2. It selects the strains according to the budget `n_max`:
   - no budget (`n_max = NULL`): one strain per optimal cluster, i.e. `k_opt`
     strains, with the status `"optimal"`;
   - budget larger than the optimum (`n_max >= k_opt`): the `k_opt` optimal
     strains, completed up to `n_max` strains (status `"supplementary"`) by
     cutting the tree into `n_max` clusters. Use `fill = FALSE` to stop at the
     optimum. As the clusters are nested, each supplementary strain comes from
     a cluster that does not contain an optimal strain yet;
   - budget smaller than the optimum (`n_max < k_opt`): the tree is cut into
     `n_max` clusters and one strain is selected in each (status
     `"selected"`). The optimal groups that are not represented by any
     selected strain are listed, so that the user knows what is missed.

In each cluster, the selected strain is the one with the largest silhouette
width, i.e. the best clustered one (ties are broken at random, use `seed` for
reproducibility).

With categorical metadata, identical strains are at distance 0, so the
optimum is often close to the number of distinct profiles. Supplementary
strains then mostly have the same metadata as already selected strains: they
do not add diversity regarding the metadata, but may be useful as replicates.

```{r examples-select_strains}
prepared_data <- prepare_input(
  salmonella_strains,
  col_select = c("CONTEXTE", "MATRICE1", "REGION", "SECTEUR", "LIEUPVT"),
  id = "IDENTIFIANT", date = "DATE_PRELEVEMENT"
)
# no budget: optimal number of strains
res <- select_strains(prepared_data, seed = 1)
res
plot(res)
# budget smaller than the optimum
res_20 <- select_strains(prepared_data, n_max = 20, seed = 1)
res_20
head(res_20$table[, c("cluster", "optimal_group", "selected", "status")])
```

## Exporting the result: export_selection

`export_selection()` returns — and optionally writes to a CSV file — the
original metadata table with the columns added by `select_strains()`. The file
can be opened in a spreadsheet and filtered on `selected` to get the list of
strains to sequence.

```{r examples-export_selection}
prepared_data <- prepare_input(
  salmonella_strains,
  col_select = c("CONTEXTE", "MATRICE1", "REGION", "SECTEUR", "LIEUPVT"),
  id = "IDENTIFIANT", date = "DATE_PRELEVEMENT"
)
res <- select_strains(prepared_data, n_max = 20, seed = 1)
selection <- export_selection(res, data = salmonella_strains, id = "IDENTIFIANT")
# the strains to sequence, with all their metadata
head(selection[selection$selected, c("IDENTIFIANT", "REGION", "status")])
# write the table to a CSV file
export_selection(res, data = salmonella_strains, id = "IDENTIFIANT",
                 file = file.path(tempdir(), "selection.csv"))
```

## Reporting: report_selection

`report_selection()` writes an HTML report of the selection: the parameters,
the silhouette curve with the optimum and the budget, the list of the
selected strains, the optimal groups that are not represented and the size of
each cluster. Together with the CSV file of `export_selection()`, it documents
the choice of the strains to sequence.

```{r examples-report_selection}
prepared_data <- prepare_input(
  salmonella_strains,
  col_select = c("CONTEXTE", "MATRICE1", "REGION", "SECTEUR", "LIEUPVT"),
  id = "IDENTIFIANT", date = "DATE_PRELEVEMENT"
)
res <- select_strains(prepared_data, n_max = 20, seed = 1)
if (requireNamespace("rmarkdown", quietly = TRUE) && rmarkdown::pandoc_available()) {
  report_selection(res, file = file.path(tempdir(), "selection.html"),
                   data = salmonella_strains, id = "IDENTIFIANT")
}
```

# Profile method

This method groups strains that are strictly identical for all the selected
metadata, and selects one strain per group. Unlike the clustering method, all
strains of a group are identical, and strains that are similar to no other
strain form a group on their own. It uses three functions: `prepare_upset()`,
`define_profiles()` and `select_profiles()`.

## Binary table: prepare_upset

`prepare_upset()` creates a binary table from the prepared data: there is one
column per modality of each metadata (named `<metadata> _ <modality>`), filled
with 1 if the strain has this modality and 0 otherwise.

```{r examples-prepare_upset}
raw_data <- salmonella_strains
prepared_data <- prepare_input(raw_data, col_select = c("CONTEXTE", "MATRICE1", "REGION", "SECTEUR", "LIEUPVT"),
                               id = "IDENTIFIANT", date = "DATE_PRELEVEMENT")
upset_data <- prepare_upset(prepared_data)
upset_data[1:5, 1:4]
```

The binary table can be used to visualise the groups of identical strains in
an UpSet plot, for instance with the {UpSetR} package:

```{r upset-plot, eval = requireNamespace("UpSetR", quietly = TRUE), fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
# the 12 most frequent modalities
UpSetR::upset(upset_data, nsets = 12, order.by = "freq", nintersects = 20,
              mb.ratio = c(0.55, 0.45), text.scale = 1.1)
```

## Groups of identical strains: define_profiles

`define_profiles()` builds a profile for each strain by concatenating the
columns of the binary table. Strains with identical profiles are put in the
same group; a profile shared by no other strain forms a group with a single
strain.

```{r examples-define_profiles}
raw_data <- salmonella_strains
prepared_data <- prepare_input(raw_data, col_select = c("CONTEXTE", "MATRICE1", "REGION", "SECTEUR", "LIEUPVT"),
                               id = "IDENTIFIANT", date = "DATE_PRELEVEMENT")
upset_data <- prepare_upset(prepared_data)
upset_profiles <- define_profiles(upset_data)
# number of distinct profiles
max(upset_profiles$group)
```

## Selecting the strains: select_profiles

Finally, `select_profiles()` selects one strain per group. A group containing
a single strain gets this strain; since all strains of a larger group are
identical, one of them is chosen at random. Use `seed` to make the selection
reproducible.

```{r examples-select_profiles}
raw_data <- salmonella_strains
prepared_data <- prepare_input(raw_data, col_select = c("CONTEXTE", "MATRICE1", "REGION", "SECTEUR", "LIEUPVT"),
                               id = "IDENTIFIANT", date = "DATE_PRELEVEMENT")
upset_profiles <- define_profiles(prepare_upset(prepared_data))
selection <- select_profiles(upset_profiles, prepared_data, seed = 1)
# one strain per distinct profile
length(unique(selection$selected))
```
